summary: Children aged 9–10 learn probability through hands-on chance experiments: predict an expected outcome, flip a coin / roll a die / draw counters many times, record each trial one-tally-at-a-time in a tally chart, and compare what happened with what was expected. Core insights: a fair device produces outcomes that cluster near but rarely exactly match the expected split, so expecting an exact match and concluding the device is biased from too few trials is the law-of-small-numbers error; each trial is independent of the last (no 'it's due' recency thinking); and a small experiment estimates rather than proves the true probability. With a fair device, running or pooling many more trials usually brings the observed proportion closer to the expected split, though not to an exact match.
misconceptions: Expecting the experiment to match the theoretical split exactly, and concluding the device is biased when it does not (law of small numbers)
Recency thinking — predicting the next trial from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, so tails is due', or 'heads is on a streak')
Recording carelessly — backfilling tallies or losing count so the total does not match the number of trials
Treating the result of a small experiment as the true probability rather than an estimate

activities.title: Predict, flip, tally: run and read a coin experiment
steps: Before flipping, predict the expected number of heads in 20 flips (about 10) and write it down.
Set up a tally chart with one row per outcome (heads, tails).
Flip the coin 20 times, marking exactly one tally per flip AS it happens — not reconstructing from memory afterward.
Total the marks and check the total equals the number of flips (20).
Describe what you notice: was it about half? Exactly ten? How close to your prediction?
activities.insight: A fair device produces outcomes clustered near the expected split but not exactly matching it; disciplined one-tally-per-trial recording is part of the procedure, and the total must reconcile with the number of trials.

activities.title: Watch the proportion settle: scale up the number of trials
steps: After a lopsided small sample (e.g. 13 heads in 20), keep going: pool results across the class, or keep flipping toward 100, 200, 500 trials.
Track both the growing tally AND the running proportion of heads as more trials accumulate.
Compare a 'small run' (20) against a 'large run' (hundreds): notice which lands closer to the expected half (usually, but not always, the large run).
State what the larger sample tells you that the small one couldn't.
activities.insight: For a fair coin, as the number of trials grows the observed proportion tends to move toward the expected split and steady; a lopsided 20-trial result can easily happen by chance with a fair coin, so on its own it is not evidence of bias. The small experiment gives an estimate, not the true probability.

activities.title: The coin has no memory: confront recency thinking
steps: After a run of several heads in a row, predict the next flip (or say it cannot be predicted) and say WHY.
Flip again and check; repeat the predict-then-flip several times.
Explain whether a streak of heads makes tails any more 'due' on the next flip.
State in your own words why each flip stays 50-50 regardless of what came before.
activities.insight: Successive trials are independent: the coin has no memory, so neither 'tails is due' (negative recency) nor 'heads is on a streak' (positive recency) is correct — each flip remains 50-50 whatever preceded it.

activities.title: Interpretation check: does a small sample prove bias?
steps: Read a completed tally showing 13 heads and 7 tails out of 20 flips.
Decide whether this proves the coin is unfair, and explain your reasoning.
Say how you could check whether the coin is actually biased.
Given a streak of four heads, say whether the next flip is more likely to be heads, more likely tails, or neither — and explain why.
activities.insight: Judging fairness and independence from a completed record: 13 of 20 heads does not prove bias because 20 trials is too few; checking requires many more trials; and no run of heads changes the next flip's odds — for a fair coin, heads and tails remain equally likely.

checkQuestion: Give the child a coin and a blank tally chart and say: 'Before you start, tell me roughly how many heads you expect in 20 flips. Now flip the coin 20 times, recording each result, then tell me what you notice.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not tell them how to record or how to interpret. Watch how they tally, whether they predict the next flip from the last few, and how they explain the gap between 'about 10' and what they actually got.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: the child predicts about half (roughly 10 heads), sets up a tally with one row per outcome, marks exactly one tally per flip AS it happens, totals 20 marks for 20 flips, and reads the result sensibly — 'about half, but not exactly ten' — treating it as close to the expected split rather than an exact match, and does not claim the next flip is 'due' to be a particular side.
